Chief Executive on Thursday José Muñoz disclosed the production target during an event in San Jose, California, InsideEVs reported. Hyundai and Waymo announced their partnership in 2024 but hadn't previously revealed the expected number of vehicles.
The robotaxis will be built at Hyundai’s manufacturing complex near Savannah, Georgia. Commercial deliveries are expected to begin in the fourth quarter, following an initial testing program.

For investors, robotaxi contracts could help Hyundai keep its U.S. factories operating efficiently as consumer EV sales fall short of earlier industry forecasts. Large fleet orders also offer more predictable volume than retail demand, though the opportunity depends on Waymo and other autonomous-driving companies expanding their services as planned.

Automakers have scaled back EV investments after slower sales growth and changes in U.S. incentives and emissions policies. Hyundai has responded by adjusting its Georgia plant to produce more hybrids while seeking additional commercial customers for its electric models.

Muñoz said Hyundai’s robotaxi manufacturing operation is already profitable and is developing into a business of its own. He also indicated that other autonomous-vehicle companies have expressed interest, potentially allowing Hyundai to expand beyond Waymo.

The Ioniq 5 vehicles will be delivered with modifications needed to accommodate Waymo’s sixth-generation autonomous-driving system. That factory integration could simplify deployment compared with vehicles that must be extensively retrofitted after assembly.
Waymo has about 4,000 vehicles operating or preparing to operate across 14 U.S. cities, according to InsideEVs. Its expansion makes the Alphabet
subsidiary a potentially significant fleet customer for automakers at a time when autonomous transportation companies are placing increasingly large EV orders.

title: Hyundai looks to robotaxis to offset slower EV demand
